newsitem.title: USA: Mkts await Greenspan's take on "Brave New World".
newsitem.headline: Mkts await Greenspan's take on "Brave New World".

text.p: U.S. financial markets are anxious to hear on Tuesday Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's version of the Brave New World that would account for the American economic dream of solid growth, full employment and low inflation.

"Is Greenspan quite as far in the Brave New World camp as people think? I don't think so. Even if he were, he would feel some need to represent the views of the other FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) members," said Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc chief economist William Dudley.
"A number of Fed bank presidents are very nervous, still, about the traditional NAIRU (non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment) view of the world," Dudley added.

Greenspan will deliver his mandatory semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on the economy and monetary policy before Congress on Tuesday beginning at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT and Wednesday at 1000 EDT/1800 GMT.

In his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony from February, Greenspan described as "transitory" the factors that led to the unusual mix of strong growth and low inflation. He also cautioned that Brave New World theories often proved to be a "mirage."
The Fed raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at its following meeting in March.

The minutes of the May FOMC minutes, the latest available, showed several FOMC numbers favoring another rate hike due to inflationary risk. The so-far favorable inflation performance, however, allowed the Fed to avoid another tightening.

"I don't think he will be conclusive on the Brave New World. He'll probably say the world is uncertain," said Dudley, adding that the markets will also try to read in the testimony whether the March hike may have been an isolated move.

Lou Crandall, chief economist at Wrightson Associates, expected any discussion about a Brave New World to be limited to the potential growth rate. He said Greenspan would avoid elaborating on the minimum jobless rate, the anchor of the NAIRU theory.
"It would be interesting if Greenspan hinted at a higher estimate of potential GDP. He could say productivity growth is not transitory," Crandall said.
"But the question is whether this also applies to the employment rate. He could warn tight labor markets may come back and bite us some day," the Wrightson economist added.
Crandall also noted a Humphrey-Hawkins testimony would not be the same unless it included a reference "to another obscure business indicator to keep us economists busy ..."
David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International, agreed the higher productivity/higher growth notion would be at the center of any New World argument.

"The Q-&-A should try to pin him down on what the new potential rate of growth is," Resler said. "Greenspan may answer this is a different, rather than a brand new world, one like in the 1960s when the U.S. economy could sustain fast growth, low unemployment and low inflation.
"Higher productivity is one explanation, but it would be interesting if Greenspan comes up with more reasons for this," Resler also said, predicting markets would focus on this.
Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp, expected Greenspan to caution that it's "too soon to conclude it's a Brave and Better New World ... rather a temporary Nirvava."
The four chief economists expected Greenspan to avoid elaborating on financial markets or their "exuberance."
